theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Who is an "entrepreneur"?
options: A person who works for a fixed wage set by a large firm
A person who lends money to businesses at a high rate
A government officer who checks business licences
A person who starts and runs a business, taking the risk

questions.stem: Which quality is most useful for an entrepreneur?
options: Waiting for others to tell you what to do
Being willing to take sensible risks and keep going
Giving up as soon as the first problem appears
Avoiding customers so that you can work quietly in peace

questions.stem: What is the main difference between being employed and being self-employed?
options: Self-employed people work for themselves and take the risk
Employed people never have to follow any rules at work at all
Self-employed people are paid a fixed wage by a boss
Employed people must find and keep their own customers

questions.stem: What is a "business opportunity"?
options: Any business that a friend is already running
A loan from the bank that must be paid back within a week
A need or problem that customers will pay to have met
A shop that is for sale at a very low price

questions.stem: Which is the best way to spot a business idea in your community?
options: Notice what people need that is hard to get nearby
Copy the busiest shop on the street exactly
Choose whichever business your cousin likes the very best
Pick an idea at random from a magazine

questions.stem: In a SWOT analysis, what does the "S" stand for?
options: Sales
Savings
Strengths
Suppliers

questions.stem: In a SWOT analysis, which of these is a "threat" to a new small business?
options: Your good skills in the trade
A loyal group of regular customers
Your savings set aside for tools
A new competitor opening next door

questions.stem: What does the "M" in a SMART goal stand for?
options: Monthly
Measurable
Marketing
Money

questions.stem: Which of these is a SMART goal?
options: Make a lot of money from the business as soon as possible
Become the very best and most famous welder in all of Jamaica
Save $50 000 for a new machine by the end of next June
Get many more customers for the business at some time soon

questions.stem: What is "market research"?
options: Finding out about customers, competitors and demand
Buying stock at the market on a Saturday morning
Putting up posters to tell people about the business
Counting the money in the cash box each evening

questions.stem: Which is a simple way for a new beauty or repair business to do market research?
options: Guess what customers want without asking any of them
Ask possible customers questions in a short survey
Wait until the business opens to find out
Only ask family members who will say yes

questions.stem: What is a "target market"?
options: Every person who lives anywhere in Jamaica
The shop where you buy your materials
The place where the business is painted and signed
The group of customers most likely to buy from you

questions.stem: Why should you study your competitors before you start?
options: So that you can copy their name and sign
To learn their prices and find how to do better
So that you can tell customers bad things about them
To find out where they live and what they earn

questions.stem: What is a "unique selling point" (USP)?
options: The lowest price that you are allowed to charge
The place where the business sells most of its goods
The first sale that a new business makes
What makes your business different from the rest

questions.stem: What is a business plan?
options: A list of the friends who will help you on opening day
A drawing of the shop sign showing its colours and shape
A written plan of the business goals, market and money
A form that is used each week to pay the staff wages

questions.stem: Why would a bank or lender want to see a business plan?
options: To judge whether the business can pay back a loan
To choose the colours used on the business sign
To decide what time the business should open
To find out the names of everyone in the owner's family

questions.stem: Which of these is a start-up cost for a small welding or salon business?
options: The bill paid every month for the electricity that is used
The wages paid to a helper each Friday
The cost of tea for the staff each week
Buying the first machine, tools and equipment

questions.stem: Which of these is a sensible source of money to start a small business?
options: A grant that every person gets without applying
A competitor's cash box
Personal savings or a small business loan
Money taken from your employer

questions.stem: Which is the best way to set the price of a service?
options: Cover all the costs, add a profit and check competitors
Charge whatever price the first customer suggests
Always charge much less than it costs you to do the job
Pick a number that sounds nice without any working

questions.stem: A job brings in $25 000. Materials and other costs come to $17 500. What is the profit?
What is "profit"?
options: The money left after all costs are paid
All of the money that customers pay to the business
The money you borrow from the bank
The price of the tools you bought

questions.stem: Which of these is a fixed cost, paid whatever the amount of work?
options: The steel used on each gate
The monthly rent for the shop
The hair dye used for each client
The welding rods used on each job

questions.stem: Which of these is a variable cost, which goes up as you do more work?
options: The yearly business registration fee
The rent for the shop each month
The insurance on the building
The materials used on each job

questions.stem: What does "break-even" mean?
options: The point where the business makes its biggest profit
The day that the business tools break and need repair
The point where income just covers all the costs
The time when the business must close for good

questions.stem: What is "cash flow"?
options: The total value of all the tools the business owns
The amount of profit made in a year
The money coming into and going out of the business
The cash that the owner keeps at home for safe keeping

questions.stem: Why should a small business keep records of all money in and out?
options: So that the owner can spend more money on personal things
So that the business never needs to pay any tax
So that the records can be shown to competitors
To know if it is making a profit and to pay tax correctly

questions.stem: What is a receipt?
options: A list of jobs that you hope to do next month
A written record that a payment was made
A letter asking a customer to pay for a job
A plan that shows how to set up a new shop

questions.stem: Why should the owner keep business money separate from personal money?
options: To see clearly how the business is really doing
So that the owner can spend business money freely
Because personal money cannot be put in a bank
So that the business never has to pay its bills

questions.stem: In Jamaica, why should you register your business name?
options: So that the business never has to pay any taxes at all
To make the business legal and protect its name
So that you can use another firm's name
Because it lets you skip all safety rules

questions.stem: In Jamaica, what does "TRN" stand for?
options: Taxpayer Registration Number
Trade Registration Notice
Training and Record Number
Taxable Revenue Notification

questions.stem: What is a "sole trader"?
options: A business owned by its shareholders and run by a board
A business owned by two or more partners together
A business owned and run by one person
A charity that helps people start a business

questions.stem: What is one disadvantage of being a sole trader?
options: The owner keeps all of the profit that the business makes
The owner makes all of the decisions without asking anyone
It is simple and cheap to set up
The owner may have to cover all debts personally

questions.stem: Which is a low-cost way for a new small business to advertise?
options: A full-page advert in a newspaper every day
A television advert at prime time
A large billboard on the highway for a year
Social media posts and word of mouth

questions.stem: What are the "four Ps" of marketing?
options: Product, price, place and promotion
People, profit, pay and the premises
Plan, purchase, pack and post
Price, payment, profit and phone

questions.stem: Why is good customer service important to a small business?
options: It allows the business to charge more than everyone
Happy customers come back and tell their friends
It means the owner never has to work hard again
It stops competitors from opening up nearby

questions.stem: What is the best way for a new business owner to reduce risk?
options: Spend all the savings on the first day
Borrow as much money as the bank will lend
Start small, plan well and keep good records
Ignore what competitors are doing in the area

questions.stem: Why might a small business take out insurance?
options: To help cover losses from fire, theft or accidents
To avoid having to pay for any of the materials at all
To make sure that it always makes a profit
To stop customers from making any complaints

questions.stem: What is "networking" for a small business owner?
options: Putting up wires for the shop's internet
Fixing computer networks for customers
Building contacts with people who can help
Selling goods and services only on the internet

questions.stem: Why should a business owner pay themselves a set wage from the business?
options: So that the business has no money left at all
So that they can take out as much as they like each day
So that no tax ever needs to be paid
To plan personal spending and keep business money safe

questions.stem: A self-employed electrician, Devon, has promised three jobs for the same day and cannot do them all. What should he have done?
options: Promised all three to make the customers happy
Planned his diary and agreed times he could meet
Turned off his phone to avoid the customers
Sent a trainee to do all three jobs alone

questions.stem: Which business practice is honest and fair?
options: Using cheaper materials than the customer paid for
Charging tourists double without telling them
Giving a written quote and sticking to it
Hiding faults in the work from the customer

questions.stem: What is a quotation (quote) given to a customer?
options: A bill that is sent to the customer after the job is finished
A written statement of the price before the job starts
A note that says the customer has paid
A list of jobs the business did last year

questions.stem: Why is it wise for a trainee to plan a path into business, such as working first to gain experience?
options: Skills, savings and contacts make success more likely
It is the only legal way to start a business
Experience in the trade is of no use in running a business
Businesses must be started before the age of 25

questions.stem: In business accounts, what is "sales turnover"?
options: The money left after all the costs are paid
The amount of stock left at the end of the day
The value of the tools and equipment owned
The total money received from sales

questions.stem: Why should a business owner review the business plan every few months?
options: Because the law says it must be rewritten each week
So that it can be shown to competitors
To check progress and change plans if needed
So that the bank will cancel the loan

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A salon sells 20 treatments at $2 500 each. What is the total sales income, in dollars?
What does the letter "T" stand for in a SMART goal?
What do we call a business owned and run by two or more people who share the profits?

What is the extra money called that you pay back on top of the amount you borrowed?

essays.stem: Describe the personal qualities of a successful entrepreneur, and explain why each one matters.
essays.modelAnswer: A successful entrepreneur is self-motivated: there is no boss to push them, so they must start work and keep going on their own. They are willing to take sensible risks, because starting a business means spending time and money without being sure of success. They are hard-working and determined, so that they do not give up when the first problems come, such as a slow month. They are creative and look for new ideas and better ways to serve customers. They are good with people, because they must deal with customers, suppliers and workers. They are organised, plan their time and keep records, so that jobs are done on time and money is not lost. They are honest, because a good name brings back customers. They are also willing to keep learning new skills.
markingPoints: Self-motivated, with a reason
Takes sensible risks, with a reason
Determined and hard-working; does not give up
Creative, good with people, organised (any two with reasons)
Honest and keeps learning

essays.stem: Explain how you would use a SWOT analysis to decide whether you are ready to start your own business in your trade.
essays.modelAnswer: SWOT stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. I would draw four boxes and fill each one honestly. Strengths are the things I am good at or have, such as my trade skills, my NVQ-J certificate, some savings or a good name with customers. Weaknesses are what I lack, such as little experience in pricing, no transport, or weak record keeping. Opportunities are chances outside me, such as many new houses being built that need grills and gates, or a new hotel that needs salon services. Threats are outside dangers, such as strong competitors nearby, rising prices of materials, or fewer customers in the slow season. I would then plan to build on my strengths, fix my weaknesses by training or working longer to gain experience, take the opportunities, and plan how to deal with each threat before starting.
markingPoints: States what SWOT stands for
Strengths and weaknesses are inside the person, with examples
Opportunities and threats are outside, with examples
Uses the analysis to plan actions (build on strengths, fix weaknesses)
Decides readiness or next steps from the result

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would take to find and test a business idea in your community.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would look around my community and listen to what people complain about or need, for example nobody nearby who repairs burglar bars quickly, or no salon open on Sunday mornings. I would make a list of a few ideas that match my skills. Next I would do simple market research. I would talk to possible customers and ask them questions in a short survey, such as whether they would use the service, how often, and what price they would pay. I would look at competitors to see their prices, quality and what they do badly. Then I would work out the costs and the likely price to see if the idea can make a profit. I might test the idea on a small scale, for example doing a few jobs at weekends, before I spend a lot of money.
markingPoints: Looks for needs and problems in the community
Matches ideas to own skills
Asks possible customers (survey or questions)
Studies competitors and works out costs and price
Tests on a small scale before spending a lot

essays.stem: List and explain the main parts of a simple business plan for a small business.
essays.modelAnswer: A simple business plan starts with a summary: the business name, what it does, the owner and the goals. The next part describes the products or services, for example making and fitting gates and grills, or nail and facial treatments. The market part says who the target customers are, what the market research found and who the competitors are, with the business's selling point. The marketing part explains the prices and how the business will reach customers, such as social media, flyers and word of mouth. The operations part covers the location, equipment, materials, suppliers and any staff. The money part gives the start-up costs, where the money will come from, the expected monthly sales and costs, and when the business should break even. The plan may end with goals for the first year and how progress will be checked.
markingPoints: Summary: name, what it does, owner, goals
Products or services described
Market: target customers, research, competitors
Marketing and prices
Operations and money: equipment, location, costs, funding, sales forecast

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the price to charge for a job or service. Use an example from your trade.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list all the direct costs of the job: the materials, for example steel, welding rods, paint and grinding discs for a gate, and the cost of my time and any helper's wages. Then I would add a share of the overhead costs, such as rent, electricity, transport and wear on tools, because the price must help pay for these too. This gives the total cost. Next I would add a profit, often as a percentage of the cost. For example, if the gate costs $20 000 in materials, labour and overheads and I add 25% profit, the price is $25 000. Finally I would check what competitors charge for similar work and what customers will pay, and adjust if needed, while making sure the price still covers all costs. I would give the customer a written quote.
markingPoints: Lists direct costs: materials and labour
Adds a share of overheads
Adds a profit (for example, a percentage)
Correct worked example
Checks competitors' prices and gives a written quote

essays.stem: Explain the difference between fixed costs and variable costs. Give two examples of each from a small business in your trade.
essays.modelAnswer: Fixed costs are costs that stay the same each month, whatever the amount of work the business does. They must be paid even in a slow month when there are few customers. Examples are the rent for the workshop or salon, the insurance, a loan repayment, and a monthly phone or internet plan. Variable costs go up and down with the amount of work. The more jobs the business does, the more it spends on them. Examples are the steel, welding rods and gas used on each job, or the hair products, nail polish and towels used for each client, and the cable and fittings for each electrical job. It is important to know both kinds of cost so that prices cover them, and so that the owner knows how much work is needed each month to break even.
markingPoints: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the work done
Two correct examples of fixed costs
Variable costs rise and fall with the work done
Two correct examples of variable costs
Why it matters: pricing or break-even

essays.stem: Describe the ways a person could raise money to start a small business. Give an advantage and a disadvantage of each way.
essays.modelAnswer: The first way is personal savings. The advantage is that nothing has to be paid back and no interest is charged. The disadvantage is that it can take a long time to save enough, and the owner may lose their savings if the business fails. The second way is a loan from a bank, credit union or a small business lender. The advantage is that the owner can get a larger amount quickly. The disadvantage is that it must be paid back with interest, even if the business is slow, and a plan and security may be needed. The third way is help from family or friends, as a loan or a gift. It may be cheaper and more flexible, but disagreements can spoil relationships. A fourth way is taking a partner who puts in money; this brings in skills as well, but profits and decisions must be shared.
markingPoints: Personal savings with an advantage and a disadvantage
Bank or credit union loan with an advantage and a disadvantage
Family or friends with an advantage and a disadvantage
Partner or grant with an advantage and a disadvantage
Points are accurate and clearly explained

essays.stem: Explain why good record keeping matters for a small business, and describe the records the owner should keep.
essays.modelAnswer: Good records show the owner how the business is really doing: how much money comes in, how much goes out, and whether there is a profit. They help the owner set prices, plan purchases and spot problems early, such as a customer who has not paid. Records are needed to pay taxes correctly, to apply for a loan, and to settle any disagreement with a customer or supplier. The owner should keep a daily record of sales and money received, with copies of receipts and invoices. They should keep all bills and receipts for things bought, such as materials, tools, rent and electricity. They should keep copies of quotations and job cards, a list of customers who owe money, a stock list, and records of wages paid. Business and personal money should be kept apart, ideally with a separate bank account.
markingPoints: Shows whether the business makes a profit
Helps pricing, planning and spotting problems
Needed for tax, loans and disputes
Names at least three records (sales, receipts, invoices, bills, stock, wages)
Keeps business and personal money separate

essays.stem: Describe the main steps to set up a small business legally in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: First the owner decides the type of business, such as a sole trader, a partnership or a company. Next they register the business name with the government office that handles business registration, so that the business is legal and the name is protected. The owner needs a Taxpayer Registration Number (TRN) and must register for the taxes that apply to the business. If they hire workers, they must register as an employer and pay the required deductions, such as national insurance, on time. They should check whether their trade needs a licence, permit or certificate, for example for electrical work or for a salon, and whether the parish council has rules for the premises. They should get suitable insurance, open a separate business bank account, and follow health and safety rules. Because rules change, the owner should check the current requirements with the right government offices.
markingPoints: Chooses the type of business
Registers the business name
Gets a TRN and registers for the taxes that apply
Registers as an employer if hiring; checks trade licences or permits
Insurance, business bank account and checking current rules

essays.stem: Describe a personal plan for moving from trainee to running your own business over the next three to five years.
essays.modelAnswer: In the first year I would finish my NVQ-J qualification and get a job in my trade, so that I gain experience and learn how a real business deals with customers, pricing and suppliers. I would set a SMART goal to save a fixed amount from each pay, for example $5 000 a month, in a separate account. In the second year I would build my skills further with short courses, and start a few small jobs at weekends to test my business idea and build a list of customers. I would keep records of these jobs. In the third year I would do market research, write a business plan, and work out the start-up costs and funding. When the plan shows the business can make a profit, I would register the business, buy the main tools and start, keeping my costs low. I would review my plan every few months.
markingPoints: Gets the qualification and work experience first
Sets SMART goals, including saving
Builds skills and tests the idea with small jobs
Does market research and a business plan before starting
Registers, starts small and reviews the plan regularly

practical1.title: Test a business idea: customer survey and SWOT poster
practical1.brief: As a group, choose one small business idea from any of the Centre's trades, for example a mobile gate and grill repair service, a home nail and lash service, a small electrical repair business, or a villa cleaning service. Together, write a short customer survey of 6 to 8 questions (for example: would you use this service, how often, what would you pay, what matters most to you). Each member then asks at least 3 people at the Centre (trainees or staff who agree to take part) and records the answers. Back in the group, count up the answers on a tally sheet. Then make a SWOT poster for the idea, using the survey results: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Each member writes at least one point on the poster and explains it to the assessor. Finish with a short written decision: go ahead, change the idea, or drop it, and why. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Paper and pens for the survey forms
A tally sheet for the results
Chart paper and markers for the SWOT poster
photos: Each member asking a person the survey questions (one photo per member, with the person's agreement)
The completed tally sheet of results
The written decision with its reasons
checklist: Helped write clear, simple survey questions
Asked at least 3 people politely and recorded their answers correctly
Helped count the results accurately on the tally sheet
Wrote at least one correct point on the SWOT poster
Explained their SWOT point clearly to the assessor
Took part in the group's decision and could give a reason for it
Worked with the group respectfully and did a fair share
safety: Survey people only inside the Centre and only if they agree; do not go into workshops while machines are running
Do not write down survey people's phone numbers or addresses
Keep chart paper, bags and cables out of walkways

practical2.title: Start-up budget, price list and quotation for a small business
practical2.brief: As a group, plan the money side of a small business in one of the Centre's trades. The assessor gives the group a business card with a list of tools, equipment and materials and their prices. First, make a start-up budget: list everything needed to open and add up the total. Next, list the monthly fixed costs (such as rent and phone) and the variable costs for one typical job or treatment. Then set prices for three services by adding up the costs of each one and adding a profit. Finally, write a quotation for a sample job that the assessor gives, showing materials, labour, profit and the total price. Share the work: each member does one part, and another member checks the sums. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the sheets once for the whole group.
materials: Business card with prices (from the assessor)
Blank budget sheet, price list sheet and quotation form
photos: The group sharing out the tasks, with the business card visible
The finished start-up budget, clear enough to read
The list of monthly fixed and variable costs
The price list for three services, showing the working
The finished quotation for the sample job
checklist: Completed their own part of the task correctly
Added up costs correctly, with the working shown
Sorted costs correctly into start-up, fixed and variable
Worked out a price that covers the costs and adds a profit
Checked another member's sums and corrected any mistake
Set out the quotation clearly: items, amounts, total and date
Explained their part to the assessor in their own words
safety: Keep phones and calculators on the table, away from the edge, and charger cables out of walkways
Use only the made-up business details on the card, not real customers' information
Sit at the tables provided and keep exits clear
